lesson_title: The Man Who Predicted an Element
hook_text: In 1869 a chemist pointed at an empty box and said: an element belongs here, it weighs about 72, and nobody has found it yet. Seventeen years later, someone did.
clip_script: St Petersburg, 1869. Dmitri Mendeleev writes every known element on a card, sixty-three of them, and plays patience with chemistry. He lines them up by the mass of their atoms and stacks the ones that behave alike in the same column. Then he does something nobody else dared. When the next card does not fit, he leaves a gap. Below silicon he says: there is a missing element here. Grey. Atomic mass about 72. Density about 5.5. In 1886 a German chemist finds germanium. Atomic mass 72.6. Density 5.35. A list that predicts the future is not just a list; it is a law of nature. Today the table is ordered by atomic number instead of mass, with eighteen groups down and seven periods across, metals on the left, non-metals top right, and the in-between semi-metals on a staircase between them. Every box is an address, and the address tells you how the element behaves.
visual_style: Whiteboard cards shuffling into columns, one empty box below silicon with a question mark, then the numbers 72 and 72.6 appearing side by side; finally an outline table with a zigzag staircase.
mood: Detective story with a satisfying reveal.
pacing: Slow build to the gap, quick reveal of the matching numbers, brisk tour of the modern table.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and find any element's address on the map.
